newsitem.title: UNITED NATIONS: U.N. approves "exit strategy" for Croatian enclave.
newsitem.headline: U.N. approves "exit strategy" for Croatian enclave.

text.p: The Security Council on Monday approved an exit strategy for U.N. personnel in Croatia's enclave of Eastern Slavonia, with the military leaving by Oct. 15 and civilians staying until January 1998.

But the council, in a resolution, left the door open for the military to remain until the mandate ends on Jan. 15, depending on Croatia's ability "to reassure the Serb population and sucessfully complete peaceful integration" as it takes back the enclave.

The once-volatile region, dominated by Serbs and bordering Yugoslav republic of Serbia, is the only Croatian area not under Zagreb's control. It seceded from Croatia in 1991, opposing Zagreb's drive for independence from Yugoslavia.

A U.N. Transitional Authority (UNTAES) has been administering the area with 5,000 troops and other personnel, as called for in the 1995 Balkan peace accords, to prevent a resumption of fighting. American Jacques Klein ran the region until his recent appointment as a deputy to the chief international representative in Bosnia, Carlos Westendorp.
Belgium, a mainstay of the U.N. force, is said to want its troops out as soon as possible.
The council in its resolution criticised Zagreb's handling of refugees wishing to return to their homes and of rights of Serbs in general.
Croatia "should eliminate promptly the administrative and legal obstacles to the return of refugees" and treat everyone equally regardless of ethnic origins, the council said.

Croatia, welcoming the resolution, nevertheless said the resolution should have spoken more about Serb crimes in the nearly obliterated Danube city of Vukovar during the independence war and the need for economic reconstruction in the region.

"Croatia does not have a problem with its minorities. It has difficulties with reintegrating one segment of one minority group that chose to take up arms," Foreign Minister Mate Granic said in a prepared statement.
According to the U.N. withdrawal plan, two battalions and one company could be repatriated by Aug. 15, reducing troop strength from 5,000 to 2,530, including 720 military support workers.
Further reductions are planned for the period after September to reach a staffing level of 720 by October, depending on developments.

The number of military observers would remain at 100, while the authorised strength of 600 civilian police officers could be reduced to the present actual strength of 450 until the full integration of the Transitional Police Force into the Croatian police force, expected in October.

The civilian police strength could subsequently be further reduced to 250, enabling a constant presence to be maintained at all police stations and two regional headquarters while monitoring the new police structure and continuing human rights training.
By October the strength of UNTAES' civilian component could be reduced to 315 international staff members from 485 and to 399 local staffers from 746, apart from 70 U.N. volunteers.
